title: Up to us, not up to us
hookLine: Epictetus opens his Handbook: some things are up to us, some are not (Enchiridion 1)

cards: No say over where you live. No say over what work you do. Not even a say over whether your body belongs to you.
The old accounts say Epictetus began life that way: born enslaved, and lame in one leg. Later he was freed, became a teacher, and was banished from Rome with the other philosophers.
If anyone had a right to say nothing is up to me, it was him. Instead, he built his whole teaching on the question of what is. A new week: the dichotomy of control.

teach.h: THE HANDBOOK: HELD IN THE HAND.
teach.b: Epictetus didn't write books. His student Arrian took notes, and later boiled the teaching down into a small handbook, the Enchiridion, which means something held in the hand, ready to use.

teach.h: SOME THINGS ARE IN OUR POWER.
teach.b: It opens like this, in George Long's 1877 translation: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. The Greek phrase is eph' hēmin: up to us, in our power. Epictetus draws the line sharply.

Up to us: our opinions, our impulses, our desires and aversions; in a word, our own acts of mind. Not up to us: our body, our property, our reputation, our office; in a word, whatever is not our own doing.

Then comes the promise. Treat as yours only what is yours, and what belongs to others as theirs, and nobody will ever force you or hinder you, and you won't blame anyone. Notice how short the first list is.
Not the weather, not the traffic, not what your boss decides, not even how your body feels today. Only how you judge and how you respond. That sounds like bad news, and at first it is.

But it's also where the relief is. A lot of worry goes into pushing on the second list: replaying what someone thinks, straining at what's already happened. Epictetus says that door doesn't open from your side.
Put your hand on the one that does.
Two columns, mine and not mine: a sorting a worried mind can do in one breath.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism sort a worry into what is up to them and what is not, following the first lines of Epictetus's Enchiridion, and put their effort only into the first.

o: fate: whatever the gods have already decided
self-control: never showing what you feel
up to us: our own judgments and our responses

p: the student who took the notes
a handbook, held in the hand

s: his student Arrian took notes and boiled the teaching down into the handbook.
Epictetus lists the body among things not up to us
body, property, reputation and office are on the not-mine list.
Epictetus was born into a wealthy Roman family
the old accounts say he was born enslaved.

games.q: you're worried a friend is annoyed with you. following Epictetus, where do you put your effort?
o: replaying what they might be thinking.
how you'll act toward them next time.
trying to control what others tell them.
games.why: what they think is not up to you. your response is. Epictetus says put your hand on the door that opens from your side.

practice: Let two or three worries come up, and take one. Ask which part is yours, your judgment, your effort, your response, and which is not, what others decide, what's already done, what happens next.
Picture each part going into its column, then rest your attention on the mine column.

wordCard.voice: Eph' hēmin. Greek for up to us, in our power: our judgments and responses, and not much else. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: up to us, in our power. The first key phrase of Epictetus's Handbook.

carryVoice: Your line: mine or not mine. One question sorts a worry into two columns. Until tomorrow.
